name: Elisabeth Elliot
title: Elisabeth Elliot: continuing to serve after loss
description: Elisabeth Elliot went back to serve in a Waorani community after losing Jim. Her story, checked against documents at Wheaton.

sections.heading: A life that went on after January 1956
paragraphs: Jim Elliot’s death in Ecuador left Elisabeth a widow and their daughter Valerie without a father. Elisabeth had developed her own missionary work. Her later story deserves to be read as the journey of a woman who made decisions, worked and wrote, and not only as part of her husband’s memory.

Wheaton College holds correspondence, manuscripts, recordings and other materials related to her years as a missionary, writer and speaker. The existence of this archive helps us follow her life through dated documents, instead of relying only on famous sayings or summarized versions of her life.

sections.heading: A dated letter from a shared life
paragraphs: A letter from October 1958 documents her arrival in a Waorani community together with Valerie, Rachel Saint, Dayuma and others. The archival catalog identifies the place beside the Tiwaenu River and describes the first days of living together. That date allows us to place her return after a process of time, learning and contacts.

Dayuma appears by name in the document. Her presence is a reminder that the relationship with the Waorani also depended on Indigenous women and their knowledge. Telling the story only as the feat of a foreign visitor would leave out people who are essential to understanding how that life together became possible.

Elisabeth died on June 15, 2015. The remembrance published by Wheaton highlights both her work in Ecuador and her writing and teaching. To value that legacy, it is wise to read her writings in their context and to distinguish her personal advice from the authority of Scripture.

reflection: Romans 12:17–21 calls us to give up revenge and to seek what is good. That passage offers a framework for reflecting on service after a loss. Grief carries real weight; a widow’s decisions should not be turned into a demand that ignores mourning, safety or the time needed to heal.

Elisabeth’s story invites us to think about forgiveness together with listening and responsibility. Those who walk alongside hurting people can offer presence, practical help and patience. The account is most fruitful when it lets us recognize everyone who took part, including those whose names receive less attention in popular biographies.
review_note: The letter’s catalog record states In Copyright. Only its catalog information is used; the document is not copied, translated or published.
